{"id": "35:14/q05", "question": "Why do the invoked fail to hear the call?", "turns_on": "Whether the referent is inert matter, a living servant with limited attention, an imagined deity, or any being's lack of divine hearing.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q05/p1", "position": "Idols are inanimate or insentient and have no capacity to hear or understand.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī distinguishes meaningful understanding from sound; Ibn Kathīr says idols have no souls. Al-Qurṭubī adds they neither see nor hear; Bursawī says hearing is not a property of inanimate matter. Al-Rāzī contrasts idols with the good word God receives at 35:10. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the statement alerts polytheists to incapacity, though they believed idols heard them."}, {"id": "35:14/q05/p2", "position": "Living holy beings may be occupied, distant, or lack independent power to hear appeals.", "reasons": "Al-Balkhī suggests angels or Jesus do not attend because they are occupied; al-Ālūsī adds distance. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says angels and holy humans hear only when God enables it."}, {"id": "35:14/q05/p3", "position": "Imaginary gods cannot hear because they do not exist.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī contrasts invented gods with actual righteous and evil beings."}, {"id": "35:14/q05/p4", "position": "No supposed god has divine ability to receive every open or secret plea, near or far.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu clarifies that the claim concerns godlike access to worshippers everywhere, rather than ordinary human hearing. Iṣlāḥī says the deities were unaware of pleas in this life and would not hear distress calls."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q06", "question": "Can angels or sanctified souls hear appeals made to them?", "turns_on": "The evidence for access to petitions by holy beings and the extent of their dependence on God.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q06/p1", "position": "There is no transmitted proof that they hear such appeals; reason allows the possibility but cannot establish it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī specifically discusses appeals from non-idolatrous callers."}, {"id": "35:14/q06/p2", "position": "They hear only when God enables them, and may be occupied with other matters.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī denies independent hearing to angels and holy humans; al-Balkhī and al-Ālūsī suggest occupation or distance."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q07", "question": "What does their failure to respond mean, even if they heard?", "turns_on": "Whether istijāba requires speech, successful aid, or acceptance of the religious claim contained in the plea; Ibn ʿĀshūr uses both verbal and practical senses.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q07/p1", "position": "They cannot speak or give a verbal answer; hearing alone does not confer speech.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī and al-Ālūsī distinguish hearing from a reply; Ibn al-Jawzī says God could grant hearing without the capacity to answer. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Iṣlāḥī note that istijāba can mean responding to a person's call."}, {"id": "35:14/q07/p2", "position": "They cannot grant requests, benefit worshippers, or avert harm.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī in Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Durr says they bring no good; Qatāda in al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī denies benefit. Al-Kāshifī glosses bringing benefit and warding off harm; Bursawī argues that one unable to benefit itself cannot benefit others. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the verb also means giving the requested thing; Ibn Kathīr says they cannot fulfill requests."}, {"id": "35:14/q07/p3", "position": "They would refuse the invocation because they reject the divinity, association or disbelief implied by it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī say idols never claim divinity; al-Bayḍāwī offers their disavowal as the alternative. Al-Qurṭubī says even living, understanding idols would obey God rather than answer a call to disbelief. Al-Biqāʿī says compliance would displease God; al-Ālūsī says close servants cannot verbally endorse a false divine status and practical aid is not their duty."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q08", "question": "Why introduce hypothetical hearing after denying it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q08/p1", "position": "It grants the worshippers' premise for argument, then points to their visible lack of response.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it anticipates the objection that idols might hear. Al-Rāzī says hearing is disputable in reason but nonresponse can be observed. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the supposition concessive and argues that repeated unanswered requests before visible idols show their incapacity or incomprehension; the worshippers cannot all be blamed as unworthy."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q09", "question": "What is meant by your shirk, and whose act is it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q09/p1", "position": "It is the worshippers' act of associating the invoked with God in divinity and worship.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī glosses it as worshipping idols; al-Rāzī compares 31:13. {"id": "35:14/q10", "question": "What do the alleged deities disown on Resurrection Day?", "turns_on": "Whether the disavowal is explained as their repudiation of worship and association or as a symbol of humanity's final perception.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q10/p1", "position": "They repudiate the worship and divine partnership attributed to them, often denying that they ordered or deserved it.", "reasons": "Muqātil links their denial of having commanded worship to 10:29; al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq phrase it as saying the people did not worship them. Qatāda says they neither accept nor acknowledge association. Al-Bayḍāwī cites 10:28; al-Nasafī 28:63; Ibn Kathīr 46:5–6 and 19:81–82; Study Quran 10:28, 59:16, 14:22 and 46:6. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes denial of invitation or approval and defines kufr as repudiation with aversion. Iṣlāḥī links the angels' denial at 34:40–41. {"id": "35:14/q11", "question": "How can the worshipped beings disavow their worshippers?", "turns_on": "Whether lifeless idols are made to speak, their state is personified, or living worshipped beings deliver the denial themselves.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q11/p1", "position": "God enables the idols or objects to speak and testify against their worshippers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says God grants cognition; al-Ṭabrisī says God makes idols speak to rebuke and deny requesting worship. Al-Balkhī says inert idols reveal the mistake as they glorify God by displaying signs of Him."}, {"id": "35:14/q11/p3", "position": "Living beings disown the worship openly according to their own standing.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī includes angels, jinn, prophets and devils and cites Jesus in 5:116. Al-Ālūsī cites angels' denial in 34:40–41. Iṣlāḥī distinguishes righteous angels and prophets, who disown worship, from evil jinn and devils, who say the worshippers chose misfortune and receive no help."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q12", "question": "Why use person-like pronouns for the invoked?", "turns_on": "Whether person-like agreement follows the idolaters' imagined personhood or a mixed group with rational beings.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q12/p1", "position": "The wording follows and mocks the worshippers' treatment of idols as discerning persons.", "reasons": "Bursawī says worshippers foolishly attributed discernment to idols and the verse predicates hearing and answering of them. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the rational relative pronoun and pronouns follow the polytheists' framing mockingly, with 35:13 in view."}, {"id": "35:14/q12/p2", "position": "The group includes rational beings, whose pronouns predominate over the idols.", "reasons": "Bursawī explicitly includes jinn and humans alongside idols as an alternative explanation."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q13", "question": "To whom is the closing address directed?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular second person identifies the Prophet specifically or serves as a general address.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q13/p1", "position": "The singular address is to the Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says God reveals an otherwise unknowable future of speaking wood and stone to him; the source is all-knowing. {"id": "35:14/q16", "question": "What does the closing maxim do?", "turns_on": "The notes identify its truth-confirming function, its role as a tadhyīl, and its proverbial form; these can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q16/p1", "position": "It certifies the preceding report because its speaker knows the idols and their future.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says only an expert gives an accurate account; al-Bayḍāwī says this confirms God's account and refutes idol claims. Al-Nasafī says God knows the causes of delusion and hidden matters; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the closing authenticates preceding reports. Iṣlāḥī urges heed of hidden truth instead of fancies; Study Quran distinguishes truths of the idols and Resurrection from what reason alone can infer."}, {"id": "35:14/q16/p2", "position": "It is a tadhyīl, a closing sentence that repeats and reinforces the argument.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī calls the close of the passage on powerless worshipped things a tadhyīl. {"id": "35:14/q17", "question": "Why are inform, like and expert worded this way?", "turns_on": "The notes address complementary features of lexical choice, ellipsis, indefiniteness and idiomatic comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q17/p1", "position": "The compact, indefinite expression generalizes the expert's unequalled authority.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the objects of inform and expert and the dimension of likeness are omitted as recoverable; indefinite khabīr under negation rules out any equal and thereby identifies the speaker. The Lubāb author says the likeness idiom does not attribute an actual likeness to God; it means no report is as reliable."}, {"id": "35:14/q17/p2", "position": "Nabaʾ is chosen for significant news, and mathl denotes an equal or similar counterpart.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says nabaʾ concerns a momentous event. He derives mathl as equality in amount, hence a double, or in quality, hence similarity, noting a rare faʿl pattern for an active participle like shibh, nidd and khidn."}]}
{"id": "35:14/q18", "question": "How is the hamza of yunabbiʾuka represented or read?", "turns_on": "The written carrier and phonetic treatment of hamza, with related cases governed by different surrounding vowels and rasm.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q18/p1", "position": "In this kasra-then-ḍamma environment, the rasm uses yāʾ for the hamza; readers differ over its realization.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says al-Akhfash's rule writes yāʾ in yunabbiʾuka and sanaqriʾuka instead of customary wāw. The majority facilitate between hamza and wāw, while al-Dānī and others following the rasm favor yāʾ substitution. He notes that a hamza without its own written shape can reflect gemination or dropping in a dialect and that comparable forms such as suʾila follow the customary rule."}, {"id": "35:14/q18/p2", "position": "For related hamza sequences, deletion with ḍamma before a following wāw is preferred by al-Dānī and rasm-following readers.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports al-Dānī's preference, while rejecting facilitation between hamza and yāʾ and replacement by wāw in that context; kasra before the wāw is weak and only three of six proposed faces are sound, including between hamza and wāw and deletion options."}, {"id": "35:14/q18/p3", "position": "Other analogues have their own rasm and sound reading rules; several proposed transfers are unsound.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī records variant omission of an alif for open hamza after fatḥa, and prefers broad allowance for arayta variation. Naʾā's nūn-and-alif rasm permits both readings at 17:83 and 41:51; raʾā's added yāʾ in two Najm instances marks imāla. At pause, yastahziʾūn-like forms allow madd, tawassuṭ or qaṣr. He rejects transferring a deletion face to ashmazzat and related forms, rejects between-between for open hamza after kasra or ḍamma while allowing the corresponding long vowel, rejects a proposed wāw alternative in raʾūf and tuʾizzuhum, and calls proposed wāw replacement in yuʾdihi baseless."}]}

{"id": "35:14/q20", "question": "What theological argument does the verse make against worshipping others?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q20/p1", "position": "Alleged gods cannot benefit or harm worshippers now and will provide no aid in the afterlife; worship belongs to God alone.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī asks why worship powerless beings rather than the Creator who controls benefit and harm and gave blessings. {"id": "35:14/q21", "question": "How does this verse figure in discussion of Qurʾānic eloquence?", "turns_on": "The notes weigh semantic arrangement and constructed imagery against mere sound or unintegrated parallel phrases.", "positions": [{"id": "35:14/q21/p1", "position": "Eloquence depends on meaningful composition and rhetorical devices, not bare phonetic ease.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī cites this verse among examples of metaphor, allusion, representation, figurative speech and concision, alongside 19:4, 2:93, 36:37, 15:94, 12:80, 47:4, 2:16, 8:58 and 8:57. He rejects ease of letters as the basis of inimitability. In Asrār he argues that rearranging Imruʾ al-Qays's opening ruins its identity; grammar and intended meanings govern order, and the perceived elegance of wording arises intellectually rather than from sound or bare lexemes. Familiar diction can independently help, while vulgarity may lie in meaning."}, {"id": "35:14/q21/p2", "position": "The strongest compositional effect joins parts into one interwoven structure rather than merely listing parallels.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī illustrates integrated paired similes with Imruʾ al-Qays, al-Farazdaq and Bashshār; he prefers Ziyād al-Aʿjam's sea comparison for subtler weaving. {"id": "35:15/q03", "question": "What does faqir mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q03/p1", "position": "A faqir is one in need, especially in severe need.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi defines it by need. {"id": "35:15/q04", "question": "How does the definite 'the poor' shape the description of people?", "turns_on": "Whether definiteness chiefly conveys intensified class identity, recalls shared knowledge, or effects a restriction relative to God.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q04/p1", "position": "It portrays people as the very class of the needy and intensifies their weakness and need.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari says an indefinite predicate would merely make them some needy people; he cites 4:28 and 30:54 on human weakness. Al-Qurtubi transmits him. Al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Biqa'i, Alusi, and Elmalili stress the encompassing or unusually intense need; Bursevi and Alusi make other creatures' need negligible by comparison. Alusi adds that jinn need less food and clothing and cites 4:28; Biqa'i adds that thought, knowledge, and intellect multiply human needs."}, {"id": "35:15/q04/p2", "position": "Its definiteness recalls an already known fact, so the statement reminds rather than first informs.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says a predicate is ordinarily indefinite, but a definite one suits a proposition whose two terms are known; everyone already knows human need."}, {"id": "35:15/q04/p3", "position": "Together with the definite subject, it restricts poverty to the addressees relative to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls it a restrictive reversal that humbles the audience, rejecting a literal absolute restriction or an asserted hyperbole as needless; he cites 39:7. Elmalili says the restriction indicates that religion and worship answer human need. Al-Tabataba'i says the deniers' reliance on idols is refuted: poverty belongs to people and richness to God; possession and lack cannot both be absent, so the wording is exclusive."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q05", "question": "How may the hamzas at 'the poor, to' be pronounced?", "turns_on": "Which of the two adjacent hamzas is eased or elided, or whether both are fully pronounced; the vowel-class note classifies the same junction.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q05/p1", "position": "Ease the second hamza; al-Khalil considers this best.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi report al-Khalil's preference at the meeting of the two hamzas."}, {"id": "35:15/q05/p2", "position": "Ease the first hamza only.", "reasons": "Listed as permitted by al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi."}, {"id": "35:15/q05/p3", "position": "Drop the first hamza.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas lists this among the permitted ways; al-Qurtubi's summary does not mention it."}, {"id": "35:15/q05/p4", "position": "Ease both hamzas.", "reasons": "Listed as permitted by al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi."}, {"id": "35:15/q05/p5", "position": "Pronounce both hamzas fully.", "reasons": "Listed as permitted by al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi."}, {"id": "35:15/q05/p6", "position": "This is an agreed instance of the fifth vowel class, damma followed by kasra.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari's Nashr counts 22 agreed occurrences in this class, including this phrase and 2:282; six others are disputed, including the Maryam address to Zakariyya and five addresses to the Prophet attributed to Nafi."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q06", "question": "In what ways are people poor toward God?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse speaks of creaturely dependence in every condition or of a distinctive human need for God's essence and attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q06/p1", "position": "Their existence, preservation, every condition, and all worldly and otherworldly needs depend on Him.", "reasons": "Yahya and al-Tabari state the general dependence; al-Tabari adds that He meets needs. Ibn Atiyya says not even an instant or a small matter is independent of Him. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Nasafi's Dhu al-Nun, Sulami's Dhu al-Nun and Junayd, Qushayri, and Study Quran stress existence, every breath or movement, and sustenance. Al-Wahidi names provision and forgiveness; Bursevi adds protection and forgiveness in the hereafter. Al-Baydawi and Alusi include people's selves and all that befalls them; Elmalili cites weakness and the trust. Al-Kashifi reads contingent essences' need for an agent; al-Tabataba'i grounds universal dependence in God's creating and governing. Al-Razi says God meets worldly and believers' future needs; Islahi likewise includes both worlds."}, {"id": "35:15/q06/p2", "position": "Human beings uniquely need God's own essence and attributes, beyond need for His acts.", "reasons": "Some Sufi authorities reported by Bursevi distinguish other creatures, which need the divine treasury or acts, from human lovers, who need the ruler's own person and attributes; the analogy is a ruler's subjects versus lovers."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q07", "question": "What kinds of poverty does the verse allow one to distinguish?", "turns_on": "Whether poverty is classified by created nature and spiritual detachment, by the object of need, or by awareness of one's need.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q07/p1", "position": "There is universal poverty of created nature and spiritual poverty through detachment.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri distinguishes dependence on the Creator for origination, sustenance, and preservation from a spiritual quality: ordinary people detach from wealth and the elect from impediments. Biqa'i transmits this and adds detachment of the heart from effects as praiseworthy poverty."}, {"id": "35:15/q07/p2", "position": "Need of God is intrinsic, while need for other things is accidental or derivative.", "reasons": "Study Quran says every felt need ultimately points to God, while needed things both veil and reveal Him. Al-Qushayri contrasts need directed to God with need for something from Him: dependence on the thing resembles sufficiency through it, while need of God becomes richness through God."}, {"id": "35:15/q07/p3", "position": "Poverty is blameworthy when one's need of God is hidden and praiseworthy when it is made visible.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports this distinction according to whether God veils or discloses the places of need."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q08", "question": "How is genuine inward poverty toward God realized?", "turns_on": "Whether realization is described by exclusive inward dependence and detachment or by recognizing divine favor as the entrance to protected poverty.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q08/p1", "position": "Depend inwardly on God alone, relinquish other attachments and self-management, and live in humble servanthood.", "reasons": "Tustari and Sahl as transmitted by Sulami, Nasafi, and Study Quran call for inward need and severance from all else; servanthood is abasement, humility, and submission. Tustari and Sulami's Sahl require primordial and present need and the death of self-management, otherwise the claim is false. Qushayri describes detachment from causes, an exclusively Godward heart, spiritual completeness without self-claim, and ease without resistance. Sulami's Junayd contrasts divine knowledge, power, dominion, and will with the servant's incapacity and need. Study Quran says recognition of divine fullness rests on recognizing one's complete poverty."}, {"id": "35:15/q08/p2", "position": "Recognizing favor opens the protected abode of poverty and need.", "reasons": "Al-Juzjani, reported by Sulami, calls poverty and need an abode of protection and recognizing divine favor its gate."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q09", "question": "What outward conduct marks the truthful poor person?", "turns_on": "Which conduct is used as the sign: dealings with goods and requests, freedom from possession, or response to affliction.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q09/p1", "position": "One neither asks nor withholds, and does not refuse or store up goods.", "reasons": "Tustari says neither asks, refuses, nor with

holds; Sa'd, reported by Sulami, has neither asks, stores, nor withholds. {"id": "35:15/q10", "question": "What spiritual value can poverty and its affliction have?", "turns_on": "Whether the benefit is humility and honor, reward beneath affliction, or a hidden divine trust.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q10/p1", "position": "Poverty is honorable and brings humility, while wealth can foster pride.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Mu'adh, reported by Sulami and Nasafi, prefers returning humbly to God over arriving with many deeds. Qushayri says humility ennobles poverty and imagined self-sufficiency abases a servant. Al-Shibli, reported by both Sulami and Nasafi, calls every affliction of poverty an honor. Bishr ibn al-Harith calls it a hidden treasure for believers, comparable to martyrdom and bestowed on those God loves."}, {"id": "35:15/q10/p2", "position": "Poverty's outward affliction conceals inward blessing and promised reward.", "reasons": "Amr al-Makki says to manifest the inner blessing and conceal the visible trial because reward is promised. Ibrahim ibn Adham says patience with poverty led him into it."}, {"id": "35:15/q10/p3", "position": "Poverty is a divine secret entrusted only to those who conceal it.", "reasons": "Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, reported by Sulami, explains that God suffices and enriches His friends and does not entrust this secret to one who discloses it."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q11", "question": "How does a servant's poverty relate to richness through God?", "turns_on": "Whether the relationship is described as need leading to God-given richness or as two mutually completing states.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q11/p1", "position": "Acknowledged need connects one to God's wealth; claiming self-sufficiency veils one from Him.", "reasons": "Tustari and Sahl as reported by Sulami, Nasafi, and Study Quran state the veil and connection. Al-Wasiti, reported by Sulami and Nasafi, says sufficiency or honor through God leaves one neither needy nor abased. Al-Husayn says greater dependence brings greater God-given richness. Al-Wasiti also contrasts concealing the Real's due, which makes one poorest, with laying it bare, which makes one truly rich. Qushayri says absence of a self-sufficiency claim brings God's enriching gift beyond sufficiency; Study Quran says full realization of divine richness requires awareness of one's poverty."}, {"id": "35:15/q11/p2", "position": "Sound need and richness through God complete each other; both belong to servanthood.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd, reported by Sulami, says neither state is complete without the other and both remain qualities of servanthood."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q12", "question": "What marks God's friends in their dependence on Him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q12/p1", "position": "They trust God, need Him, and return to Him in everything.", "reasons": "Tustari reports this from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. Nasafi reports the same triad anonymously as three marks of the saints."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q13", "question": "Why does the verse explicitly say 'to God'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q13/p1", "position": "Dependence belongs to God alone, so worship and reliance must be directed to Him alone.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says the added phrase excludes worship of anything on which people do not depend. Elmalili says only God can satisfy human need and no other deity merits worship; he points to 35:13, where other supposed owners possess not even a qitmir. {"id": "35:15/q14", "question": "What is the syntactic role of 'He'?", "turns_on": "Whether huwa is syntactically extra or begins a new nominal clause.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q14/p1", "position": "It is an extra or separating pronoun without a syntactic position.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi give this analysis as a possibility."}, {"id": "35:15/q14/p2", "position": "It is the nominative subject of a nominal sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi give this as the other possible analysis."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q15", "question": "What does God's being 'the Rich' affirm?", "turns_on": "Whether independence is stated absolutely or restricted to the immediate addressees and their worship.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q15/p1", "position": "God alone is absolutely self-sufficient, needing no creature, helper, worship, or service.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Biqa'i, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalili, Islahi, Kuran Yolu, and Study Quran variously stress freedom from all beings and their worship. Al-Tabataba'i grounds it in creation and governance and says God can dispense with or replace people. Bursevi contrasts rulers needing servants and merchants needing carriers; al-As'ila al-Muqhima says creating, sustaining, or charging creatures changes no divine need. Islahi says God's relation to them is mercy and favor, and cites a Persian couplet that creation displays generosity rather than divine benefit. Al-Alusi prefers this broader sense over al-Tibi's restricted formulation."}, {"id": "35:15/q15/p2", "position": "He is independent specifically of the addressees and their worship, since other servants praise Him.", "reasons": "Al-Tibi's narrower formulation is reported by al-Alusi, who explicitly prefers the broader sense of complete independence."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q16", "question": "Does divine wisdom require God to charge people to know and thank Him?", "turns_on": "Whether obligation or creation supplies any benefit or protection to God, which Bursevi denies.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q16/p1", "position": "No; creation and command serve no divine benefit or protection from harm.", "reasons": "Bursevi says making creation serve God's benefit or avert harm contradicts His independence; he compares a protective rationale to the Magian claim that angels shield God from Satan. Al-As'ila al-Muqhima says creating or not creating and commanding or not commanding are alike with respect to divine independence."}, {"id": "35:15/q16/p2", "position": "The Mu'tazili claim makes divine wisdom require charging people to know and thank God.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports and rejects this claim because it would make creation serve a benefit or avert harm."}, {"id": "35:15/q16/p3", "position": "The Magian claim says angels were created to protect God from Satan.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites and rejects it as an analogy for the notion that God created beings to protect Himself."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q17", "question": "What does 'the Praiseworthy' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether praise is explained through received favors, all divine acts and their wisdom, or an intrinsic quality independent of actual praisers.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q17/p1", "position": "God is praised and deserves thanks for His favors and beneficence.", "reasons": "Yahya says creatures praise God and are charged to do so. Al-Tabari says all blessings are His and praise is due in every circumstance, citing 14:1. Al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalili, and Kuran Yolu connect praise to beneficence; Nasafi says every tongue praises Him. Alusi says hamid originally means 'praised' and cites Ka'b al-Ghanawi's line about a forbearing man respected by an enemy. Bursevi's al-Kashifi calls manifestation of divine names through beings a favor meriting praise. Study Quran's al-Maybudi says only those fully aware of their poverty truly praise Him."}, {"id": "35:15/q17/p2", "position": "God is worthy of praise in every act, word, decree, and law, including giving and withholding.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi says all divine acts merit praise. Ibn Kathir extends it to everything God says, decrees, and legislates. Biqa'i says all creation is made fittingly and at its appointed measure; blame comes from isolating parts. His report from al-Harali defines praise as the whole's perfection when all parts reach their ends, and al-Ghazali's parallel describes a human praiseworthy in all habits, character, and deeds. Biqa'i adds that both giving and withholding follow subtle wisdom without self-interest."}, {"id": "35:15/q17/p3", "position": "God's praiseworthiness is intrinsic and remains whether or not anyone praises Him.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says He is praiseworthy with or without creatures. Ibn Atiyya calls Him absolutely praiseworthy. Study Quran makes praise intrinsic to the Divine Nature; Islahi calls Him praiseworthy in His attributes."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q18", "question": "Why pair 'the Rich' with 'the Praiseworthy'?", "turns_on": "Whether the added epithet chiefly explains the benefit of divine wealth or makes explicit the duty of grateful worship despite divine independence.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q18/p1", "position": "Divine wealth benefits the needy because God gives generously, so recipients praise Him.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi say wealth alone benefits no one without generosity. Abu Hayyan, Nasafi, Alusi, and Ibn Ashur apply the same pairing to God. Al-Qushayri says He gives until praised and that Hi

{"id": "35:15/q19", "question": "Whose need does the call to worship serve?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q19/p1", "position": "Worship and accepting the call benefit people; God has no need of their response.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says people should worship and seek God's pleasure because He meets their needs. Elmalili says religion and worship meet human need; Kuran Yolu calls worship an innate, irrepressible human inclination. {"id": "35:15/q20", "question": "What occasion is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q20/p1", "position": "After the Prophet repeatedly prayed while unbelievers persisted in rejection, they asked whether God needed their worship; the verse answered them.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this occasion but says it does not restrict the verse to that circumstance."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q21", "question": "Why remind people of poverty before declaring divine independence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q21/p1", "position": "It humbles an arrogant audience and draws out an implication of dependence they know but neglect.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says proofs and reminders have failed and may feed arrogance; placing human need first is more humbling than merely asserting God's independence and may awaken sound minds veiled by misguidance. Some persistent unbelievers instead meet life with bewilderment and bitterness, unlike the praise of ancestors and idols formerly heard. Nasafi says naming poverty directs them toward dependence rather than demeaning them."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q22", "question": "How is the eloquence of this verse assessed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q22/p1", "position": "Its eloquence, like that of the Qur'an as a whole, cannot be fully expressed.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says some passages' eloquence appears more clearly to readers because of their own limitations."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q23", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding passage and surah?", "turns_on": "These are different links: the immediate warning, an earlier national example, and a gloss on the next verse.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q23/p1", "position": "It intensifies the prior warning: only God creates and governs, idols own nothing, and He can replace those who reject Him.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i connects the verse to proofs of God's creation and governance, false gods' lack of ownership, and the following threat of replacement as recompense. Ibn Ashur points to the preceding polytheists and says Islam will find other adherents. Islahi says verses 15–17 intensify the earlier admonition. Study Quran describes the surah's focus on the sole Creator and Sustainer against idol claims. Elmalili invokes 35:13 and its qitmir image."}, {"id": "35:15/q23/p2", "position": "Sheba earlier exemplifies a nation that answered favor with arrogance and lost its blessings.", "reasons": "Islahi says Sheba fulfilled Satan's prediction, suffered exemplary punishment and deprivation, and became a tale of the ancients."}, {"id": "35:15/q23/p3", "position": "In the following verse, 'bi-aziz' means beyond God's power or impossible for Him.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari glosses the following verse's wording this way."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q24", "question": "How does receiving charity bear on the poor person's role?", "turns_on": "The report ranks giver and receiver; the author's explanation identifies the receiver's necessary role in giving.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q24/p1", "position": "The giving hand is better than the receiving hand.", "reasons": "Burhan reports the Prophet defining the upper hand as the giver and the lower as the receiver, with the loan verse 2:245 offered as support."}, {"id": "35:15/q24/p2", "position": "The receiving hand enables the giver's charity and purification.", "reasons": "Burhan says charity depends on a recipient accepting the due owed to God; without receiving, a wealthy person could not give."}]}
{"id": "35:15/q25", "question": "How does Qur'anic poverty differ from bu's and ba'sa?", "turns_on": "Whether al-Raghib's proposed lexical associations fit the Qur'anic distribution of ba'sa, ba's, and faqr.", "positions": [{"id": "35:15/q25/p1", "position": "Faqr is expressly contrasted with divine wealth; Qur'anic ba'sa denotes adversity, and ba's denotes war or force.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati cites 3:181, 24:32, 35:15, and 47:38 for faqr versus wealth, 2:177, 2:214, and 3:140 for ba'sa with adversity, and 6:65 and 4:84 for ba's in fighting, force, and dominance."}, {"id": "35:15/q25/p2", "position": "Al-Raghib associates bu's especially with poverty and war, and ba's or ba'sa with attack.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports al-Raghib's lexical distinction and objects that the cited Qur'anic usages pair ba'sa with adversity and explicitly oppose faqr to wealth."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q01", "question": "How does 'when We sent' connect grammatically to the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the second time clause restates the first or supplies the time of the messengers' arrival.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q01/p1", "position": "It is apposition to the earlier 'when they came' in 36:13, explaining the arrival as a sending.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi calls it apposition; al-Nasafi and Bursevi identify the second idh as apposition to the first. Al-Tabataba'i and Islahi say it elaborates the earlier mention of messengers coming. Al-Razi reports this possible parsing."}, {"id": "36:14/q01/p2", "position": "The time clause modifies 'they came': they came when God sent them.", "reasons": "Al-Razi prefers this as clearer and stresses that the messengers did not arrive on their own initiative."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q02", "question": "Who sent the messengers, and were they prophets or Jesus's disciples?", "turns_on": "The force of God's 'We sent' and the people's objection to human messengers, weighed against reports that Jesus acted under God's command and whether the miracles prove prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q02/p1", "position": "Jesus sent his disciples under God's command, so God attributes their commission to Himself.", "reasons": "Qatada's account names Antioch and says Jesus sent two disciples then a third; Ibn Jurayj and others say an envoy of God's messenger can be called God's envoy. Al-Thalabi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Bursevi, Elmalili and Study Quran explain the attribution through God's authorization. Al-Razi says their rejection consoles Muhammad as rejection of him. Al-Alusi answers the objection from their miracles: these may be Jesus's confirming signs through representatives. Al-Tabrisi cites Wahb and Ka'b; al-Ayyashi's variant says Jesus sent his legatee Shimon to rescue the first two. Bursevi infers that on this account the apostles were not prophets. Al-Razi and Bursevi compare an authorized subagent, whom the principal may dismiss but the intervening agent may not. Ibn Jurayj reports that Jesus sent the two men to the town."}, {"id": "36:14/q02/p2", "position": "God sent prophets directly; the words describe divine messengers in their own right.", "reasons": "The apparent 'We sent' favors this reading for Ibn al-Jawzi, Elmalili and al-Alusi. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi point to the people's objection that the men were mere humans; Islahi adds their sworn claim in 36:16. Al-Alusi cites miracles as an argument proper to prophets, and says one scholar saw them as confirming Jesus's law as Aaron supported Moses. Study Quran cites mursal for Muhammad in 36:3 and 2:252 and its use for other prophets. Al-Tabataba'i's transmitted variant distinguishes God's three envoys from Jesus's later dispatch of Shim'un."}, {"id": "36:14/q02/p3", "position": "The first two are Moses and Aaron, with Moses the primary messenger and Aaron his assistant.", "reasons": "Islahi says they are the sole pair sent simultaneously to one people in prophetic history, as earlier surahs discuss; his account identifies the supporting third as Pharaoh's believing kinsman and treats the plural claim as collective embassy speech."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q03", "question": "When were Jesus's disciples dispatched?", "turns_on": "The transmitted chronology of Jesus's ascension and the disciples' dispersion.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q03/p1", "position": "They were sent after Jesus was raised to heaven.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi dates the event to the raising. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add that one made to resemble Jesus was crucified and the disciples dispersed. Al-Qurtubi and Elmalili also place the sending after the raising."}, {"id": "36:14/q03/p2", "position": "God ordered Jesus to send the apostles to cities before his ascension.", "reasons": "Kashf al-Asrar, as reported by Bursevi, says two went to Antioch before the ascension."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q04", "question": "To which place and people were the messengers sent?", "turns_on": "Whether the traditional Antioch account fits the Quranic destruction and the later h

istory of Christianity there.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q04/p1", "position": "They went to idol-worshipping Antioch and its people.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, Qatada, tafsir reported by al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kathir and many others name Antioch. {"id": "36:14/q05", "question": "Why does the verse say 'to them' rather than 'to the town'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q05/p1", "position": "Sending properly takes people as its destination, and naming the people prepares for their rejection.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi notes that rejection also attaches more clearly to people; the explanatory fa resembles the sequence after Moses struck the stone and water gushed forth in 2:60."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q06", "question": "Who were the first two messengers?", "turns_on": "Conflicting transmitted names; some commentators decline identification because no Quranic or sound-hadith name settles the matter.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q06/p1", "position": "They were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb give these names; spelling varies as Ṣadūq/Sadduq, and the third is Salūm/Shalūm. The reports through Ibn Ishaq also name Antioch and its king. Al-Nasafi includes their meeting with Habib."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p2", "position": "They were Shimʿūn/Simon and Yūḥannā/John.", "reasons": "Shuʿayb al-Jubbāʾī, Shu'ba and others identify this pair and call the third Paul; spellings of Simon and John vary."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p3", "position": "They were Yaḥyā and Yūnus.", "reasons": "Wahb and al-Baydawi report this pair; Bursevi holds it and says the mission was by God's command. Al-Baydawi also reports the unelaborated alternative that they were others."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p4", "position": "They were Yūḥannā/John and Būluṣ/Paul.", "reasons": "Wahb and some later reports give this pair; Elmalili's reported combination makes Simon Peter the third."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p5", "position": "They were Tūmān and Yūnus.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives these names in his account."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p6", "position": "They were Ṭārūs and Mārūs.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives the pair in al-Tha'labi."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p7", "position": "They were Tūmān and Mānūs.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi reports this as Muqatil's naming; the Muqatil notes elsewhere give Tūmān and Yūnus or Būluṣ, so the transmitted second name varies."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p8", "position": "They were Simʿān and Yaḥyā.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqash supplies these names."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p9", "position": "They were Tūmān and Būluṣ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Alusi attribute this pair to Muqatil."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p10", "position": "They were Nāzūs and Mārūs.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi lists this as another reported pair."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p11", "position": "They were Moses and Aaron.", "reasons": "Islahi argues that only these two were sent simultaneously to one people and that Moses was primary while Aaron helped."}, {"id": "36:14/q06/p12", "position": "Their names cannot be established from the Quran or sound hadith.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says reports of the names and treatment conflict; it cites Ibn Atiyya's decision to omit unreliable material. Al-Baydawi reports an unspecified alternative to Yaḥyā and Yūnus."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q07", "question": "Why were two messengers sent together?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q07/p1", "position": "Each could support and strengthen the other's mission.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says the two mutually supported the call to faith; Islahi's Moses–Aaron reading likewise treats Aaron as Moses's assistant."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q08", "question": "How did the townspeople first respond to the two messengers?", "turns_on": "The verse states denial; further reports differ on the physical treatment, while later words explain the people's objection to human envoys.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q08/p1", "position": "They denied the two, and reports say they beat or imprisoned them.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says both beating and imprisonment. Wahb says the king jailed them and ordered one hundred lashes; other accounts say beating or imprisonment. The denial persisted despite signs, according to al-Biqa'i.
